I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: The trigger profile mixes tactile/startle-type cues and driving-with-others cues that could fit war-zone trauma, but 'being looked at sexually' points toward a sexual-threat trauma context that is not supported elsewhere in memory, threat, or appraisal items. This specific trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The dominant threat items describe generalized vigilance and fear of interpersonal attack. In combination with the sexual-objectification trigger, this pulls the profile toward an interpersonal/sexual trauma formulation, whereas the memory and appraisal items do not contain corresponding themes. This creates cross-node incoherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear link to the other selected items. The rest of the appraisals center on unfairness, shame, and inability to trust oneself; without any role-related trauma content in memory, triggers, or threat, this item feels weakly anchored and clinically mismatched relative to the otherwise war-zone/interpersonal-danger presentation.

vignette: Five years ago, Aroha's civilian transport was caught in an ambush outside a fractured border region. She had been riding with neighbors when an IED detonated beside the bus, the concussive blast throwing bodies against hers and leaving her pinned beneath twisted metal. Over the following months, she watched civilian camps burn and heard relentless artillery that never gave warning, a chaos that stripped her of any control. When she finally returned to her home in Washington state, of Māori and Samoan descent, the war did not stay in the past. At first, it lived in the gaps of her nights. She would lie awake, her muscles coiled tight, convinced she needed to stay alert for the next attack. Even in her own bed, her eyes darted to the window, her body constantly scanning for danger she could not see but somehow knew was near. She could not relax, not even when her husband, Leo, would gently cover her shoulder with his hand. The very weight of his arm against hers made her flinch so violently that she would shove away, certain that anyone near her was a threat before they could be a comfort. That sudden tactile shock would pull the fragmented pieces of that ambush straight into her mind. She did not get a coherent story; she got shards of heat, the smell of burnt rubber, and the feeling of being trapped. When a stray dog snapped while she was treating it at the clinic, or a truck backfired outside the examination room, the sudden noise or the unannounced brush of a technician's sleeve against her arm instantly triggered the old shame and helplessness. She told herself she could not trust her own reactions, that she had failed when it mattered most, and that the universe had abandoned her to random violence. But those negative judgments did not fade; they colored how she recalled the event, filling the gaps in her recall with darker fragments of helplessness. Believing she could not rely on herself to stay safe turned every loud sound into a precursor to another ambush. The memory of that helplessness fed back into the present, making ordinary triggers feel like life-or-death alerts. She had come to believe that safety was an illusion, and that her own judgment was fundamentally unreliable. What frightened her most was not the noise itself, but what the noise convinced her was coming next. She would pause her work mid-procedure, her breath catching as the clinic's fluorescent hum seemed to mimic distant mortar fire. This constant state of alert kept her from relaxing, and that unrelenting physical tension only convinced her again that she could not rely on herself to find safety. The conviction that bad things were inevitable made her reinterpret her own memories, turning the shame of recall into proof of her helplessness. When the fragmented pieces of the ambush finally surfaced, they did not merely flash; they commanded her attention, sharpening her fear of loud noises and unannounced touch. As she tried to navigate her days, the negative appraisals she clung to acted as a filter, ensuring that any sudden contact or mechanical bang would instantly reactivate the old narratives of unfairness and betrayal. The memory of that day did not just return; it pulled her straight back into the hypervigilant state that had governed her nights for years. And as her body refused to unwind, keeping her perpetually tense, the exhaustion only reinforced her belief that the world was deeply unjust and that she was entirely alone in facing it. She avoided driving with passengers, riding shotgun alone in her truck, and she stopped attending community gatherings, citing clinic emergencies. Over months, the isolation calcified into a quiet exhaustion. She knew she was drowning in a loop she could not name, but she could not see how to step out of it until a routine spay surgery turned into a panic attack when a monitor beeped too loudly. Now, sitting across from me, Aroha explains that the final push came when she dropped a scalpel during an examination and couldn't pick it up because her hands were shaking so badly. What she is most afraid of is losing her composure again, either in the clinic or in her marriage, but what she is most hoping for is to remember the war without feeling the weight of it in her bones.
